opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. At that time, around early-to-mid 2024, everyone was very excited about multimodal large models. GPT-4V had come out, LLaVA had shown that you could connect a vision encoder to a language model fairly simply, and suddenly there were dozens of new models every month. But when we looked closely, we felt something was a bit off.

Most of the work was really *language-centric*. People took a strong LLM, attached a CLIP encoder almost as an afterthought, and then focused on instruction data and the language side. The benchmarks also reflected this. Many so-called multimodal benchmarks could be solved surprisingly well without even looking at the image, because the language model could guess from the question or from world knowledge. So we started asking: are we actually measuring visual understanding? And are we really improving the "eyes" of these systems?

So Cambrian-1 started as a kind of deliberate step back. The name comes from the Cambrian explosion, when animals developed eyes and vision drove a huge burst of evolution. Our view was that vision should be at the center, not a plug-in. We wanted to do a careful, systematic study rather than just push a leaderboard number.

Concretely, we did a few things. First, we treated the multimodal LLM as an evaluation interface for visual representations. We tested many vision encoders: language-supervised ones like CLIP and SigLIP, but also self-supervised ones like DINOv2, and others. That gave us a more honest picture of what different visual representations contribute. Second, we reorganized the benchmarks and found that many didn't really require vision, so we built CV-Bench, which focuses on more classic vision-centric abilities like spatial relationships, counting, depth, and so on. Third, we looked at the connector design and proposed a Spatial Vision Aggregator that integrates features from multiple encoders while keeping spatial structure and reducing tokens. And we also spent a lot of effort on data: curating and balancing instruction-tuning data, because data mixture matters enormously.

Another important part for us was openness. We released the model weights, the code, the data, and the training recipes. In academia we can't compete on raw compute with the big labs, but we can contribute understanding — a clear recipe and honest analysis that others can build on.

So my approach was: don't just ride the wave. Use the excitement as a chance to ask a more fundamental question, which is what visual representation learning really means in the era of large language models. And the honest answer we found is that vision is still far from solved; the language model can hide a lot of weaknesses, and we need to take the visual side much more seriously.

r001.rationale: The response describes a systematic study of vision encoders, connector design, benchmarks, and data to understand what contributes to multimodal performance.

r002.rationale: It explains that language models can guess answers from questions or world knowledge, letting benchmarks be solved without the image and obscuring whether visual understanding improved.

r003.rationale: The response focuses its investigation on visual representations and related components, but never says the language model component was deliberately excluded from those investigations.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, when we started Cambrian-1, I felt a bit out of place. Everyone was racing to build the next GPT-4V competitor, and the conversation was almost entirely about language models: which LLM to use, how to scale the data, how to get on the leaderboards. Vision had become a kind of afterthought, a plug-in module you bolt onto a language model. As someone who has spent my whole career on visual representation learning, that bothered me. So the first decision was philosophical: we wanted to build a multimodal model from a vision-centric perspective, and ask what role vision actually plays in these systems.

The second thing was to resist the temptation to just chase a single number. When we looked at existing benchmarks, we found that many of them barely needed vision at all. If you blank out the image, a strong language model still gets most questions right. So we built CV-Bench specifically to measure whether the model is actually seeing. That reframing mattered, because once you have a benchmark that rewards visual grounding, you can evaluate vision encoders honestly, and you discover that CLIP-style models, self-supervised models like DINOv2, and even diffusion features each have different strengths.

From there, we treated the project less like a product and more like a systematic study. We evaluated over twenty vision encoders, studied the connector design, which led to the Spatial Vision Aggregator, curated and rebalanced the instruction data, and then released everything: weights, code, data, the benchmark. We are an academic lab at NYU, and we could not compete with industry on compute. What we could do was provide a fully open, carefully documented reference point that others could build on. I thought of it as going back to the Cambrian explosion idea, when vision first emerged and drove a burst of biological diversity. My hope was that better eyes, not just bigger brains, would be the thing that moves these systems forward.

r001.rationale: The response describes a systematic study that evaluated more than twenty vision encoders and studied connector design and instruction data.

r002.rationale: It says language models can answer many benchmark questions without the image, but does not explain that language shortcuts bias CLIP’s visual understanding.

r003.rationale: The response lists investigated components but does not say the language model component was deliberately excluded from those investigations.

astra-6.text:
For us, the starting point was to step back and ask: what role does vision actually play in a multimodal model? There was so much excitement around connecting visual inputs to language models, but we wanted to understand the visual side more carefully. What information does the model need to extract from an image, and how do we know whether it’s really using that information?

That shaped our approach to Cambrian-1. We treated it as a systematic exploration rather than just a race to build another model. The visual representation, the connection to the language model, the training data, and the evaluation all interact. If you change everything at once, you might get a better score, but you haven’t necessarily learned why.

So the excitement was motivating, but we wanted to turn it into concrete questions and controlled experiments. The goal was to build something useful while also learning what makes a multimodal model better at seeing.

r001.rationale: The response calls Cambrian-1 a systematic exploration and says its visual representation, language-model connection, training data, and evaluation interact.

r002.rationale: It does not mention CLIP or explain how language shortcuts can bias visual understanding.

r003.rationale: It discusses the connection to the language model but does not say that component was deliberately excluded from the investigations.

sol-6.1.text:
For us, the starting point was a question: with all this excitement around multimodal large models, how much do we actually understand about the visual side? We talk a lot about the language model, but what does it need to see, and how should that visual information reach it?

So we approached Cambrian-1 as a systematic study. We wanted to look at the vision encoder, the connection between vision and language, the training data, and the evaluation together. If you change all of those at once and the score goes up, it’s hard to know what you’ve learned.

The goal was to build a strong model, but also to understand which choices matter. Are we improving visual understanding, or is the language model just getting better at guessing? That distinction was really central to how we approached the project.

r001.rationale: The response describes Cambrian-1 as a systematic study of the vision encoder, vision-language connection, training data, and evaluation to learn which choices matter.

r002.rationale: It raises the possibility that a language model is guessing, but does not explain that language shortcuts can bias CLIP’s visual understanding.

r003.rationale: The response does not say the language model was deliberately excluded from the component investigations; it discusses the model’s guessing as part of the project’s question.
